response.query: How should we design group allocation and sample size to detect sex‑by‑treatment interactions if both male and female rats are included?
response.answer: To detect sex-by-treatment interactions in rats, allocate equal numbers of male and female rats to each treatment group, and use a sample size large enough to achieve sufficient statistical power, typically guided by power analysis.

results.title: Behavioural investigations of psilocybin in non-human animals 1962 ...
results.content: OLMSTEAD5, CRAIG GOLDIE7 and ERIC DUMONT4 1 Centre for Psychedelics Health and Research at Providence Care, 752 King St. W., Kingston, ON, K7L 4X3, Canada 2 Department of Psychiatry, Queen’s Health Sciences, Queen’s University, Canada 3 University of Groningen, Groningen, the Netherlands 4 Department of Biomedical and Molecular Sciences, Queen’s University, Canada 5 Department of Psychology, Centre for Neuroscience Studies, Queen’s University, Canada 6 Bracken Health Sciences Library, Queen’s University, Canada 7 Department of Oncology, Queen’s University, Canada Received: December 30, 2023 • Revised manuscript received: July 3, 2025 • Accepted: July 18, 2025 Published online: September 11, 2025 ABSTRACT Background and Aims: Psilocybin is a psychedelic compound that may hold promise for a wide range of human health conditions, yet the identification of therapeutic processes and mechanisms of action remains exploratory. We conducted a scoping review of pre-clinical behavioural investigations of psi-locybin in non-human animals to identify behavioural effects, studies completed, behavioural tests employed, and what dosing modalities had been studied. All studies reported behavioural outcomes following drug administration, with ﬁfty-one studies (66.2%) using psilocybin, thirty studies (42.9%) psilocin, four studies (5.2%) administering whole mushroom extracts (WME), and a further eight studies investigating both psilocybin and psilocin and one study reporting the effects of both psilocin and WME.
